prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, and its development to a fractional uncertainty of about 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B012 as a single two-person part. The scientific content is one idea followed by one decisive demonstration: the magic-wavelength lattice makes the trap shift both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free without perturbing the transition, and Ye's group then took strontium to the 10^-18 regime with ultrastable lasers and systematics control. The performance has been reproduced by several laboratories and species for years, the interpretation is not contested, and it has already changed what can be tested: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and the evidence base for redefining the second. The 2005 comb prize made optical clocks countable but did not cover this step. The round-1 files show that every member who engaged with B012 accepts Katori and Ye as the natural pair and accepts the 10^-18 result as secure, so the live question is only whether a precision-measurement invention is prize-level, and I think it is, because it changes what physics can be measured. I also take the chair's questions on the citation seriously and have reworded mine around the lattice-clock architecture and not around record numbers or clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The credit is a simplification. Trapped-ion clocks, the Sr groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, the JILA team members, and Hall and Haensch on the comb and laser side all contributed to the regime that a Katori-Ye citation points at, and I cannot verify from the supplied text that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal has priority over contemporaneous ideas. The SI second has not been redefined. And B022 is the broader scientific story: a quantitative prediction in 2011 followed by correlated and superconducting states in 2018, reproduced widely, with seven of eight members ranking it in their top three. If the committee could establish that the experimental credit for B022 is adequately captured by the supplied names, and decide that eight years is enough, I would not block it. At present I cannot establish either, so I rank it second.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B022 as the best-supported prize, noted that all eight members proposed the same three names, and asked that the author record of the first 2018 reports be examined, since Dean's group is the most serious omission.
responses.response: I agree that the question about the author record is the right one, and it is the point on which my ranking turns. I cannot settle it from the supplied materials, and my recollection that the first author of the 2018 papers was a doctoral student in Jarillo-Herrero's group, with other groups contributing important early confirmation, is only a recollection. Agreement of all eight members on three names shows that the supplied strings are uncontested, not that the credit has been tested against the record. Your own comparison of B012 as the strongest alternative is fair, and I would add that if the author-record check shows that credit for the experimental discovery cannot be limited to one group without arbitrariness, that moves B022 below B012 on attribution grounds alone, which is what your first question to the committee already allows.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the unresolved superconducting mechanism concerns interpretation and not the discovery, that scope should outweigh clean attribution, and that a precision instrument improves an existing capability while B022 opened a new class of phenomena.
responses.response: I accept the first point: existence and mechanism are separate, and we have honoured results before their microscopic explanation was complete, so I do not treat the open pairing mechanism as disqualifying. I do not accept that the clock only improves an existing capability. Going from a few ions to thousands of atoms at 10^-18 changed the kind of measurements that are possible, because gravitational redshift across a millimetre is now resolved in one sample, and that is a new capability, not a refinement. On scope versus attribution I agree they can conflict, but a prize also has to name people, and for B012 the names are short and defensible while for B022 you yourself carry Dean as an open point. You said you would move to B012 if the credit problem is unresolvable, and I think that sentence marks the real difference between us, which is about evidence we do not have, not about physics.

responses.point: Mehlig weighs the lasting benefit of a new regime of matter more heavily than an outstanding instrument, but says he would not oppose the clocks if the committee prefers cleaner attribution, and calls B012 the best-defined two-person configuration.
responses.response: I value that you describe B012 as the best-defined configuration, because that is the claim I am making. On the type of discovery, I would say the criterion is lasting benefit through new understanding and that a clock comparison at 10^-18 delivers understanding directly: it tests relativity, constants and dark-matter couplings at a level no earlier instrument reached, so it is a discovery tool as much as an instrument. Your point that experimental credit in modern materials work is often shared and has not stopped the committee before is fair, but here the three-person rule forces the cut within a dispute we cannot yet resolve, whereas the clock has no comparable cut within the two names. I agree with you that a citation for B022 should lean on the transport and scanning-probe evidence and not only on the prediction.

responses.point: Eriksson cautions that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives flat bands but does not predict the correlated phases, and says he would accept B012 if the committee wants a prize without an attribution dispute, but that safety should not decide the ranking.
responses.response: Your caution about the theory credit matters to me: if the continuum model is a band-structure result, then the theory-predicts-experiment narrative that gives B022 much of its appeal is weaker than it sounds, and the citation would have to be written so that it does not imply the prediction of superconductivity. I also agree that safety alone should not decide the ranking, and it does not for me. My preference rests on a positive scientific argument, namely a new many-atom architecture that made the 10^-18 regime reachable, and on the fact that it has been independently confirmed for years, which settles interpretation as well as credit. I would put it that waiting on B022 costs little, because your own point that a few more years would settle both interpretation and credit applies to a field whose phenomena are not going away.

responses.point: Kroll proposed that the citation say explicitly that the award is for the lattice-clock architecture and its 10^-18 realisation, and treats the pending redefinition of the second as supporting evidence of impact, not as a criterion.
responses.response: I agree with both points and have adopted the wording in my citation: it names the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength interrogation of many atoms, and refers to 10^-18 only as the level reached, so ion-clock, comb and other lattice-clock contributors are not implied to be lesser. On the redefinition, I take your view and Johansson's concern together: the redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies that follows from the demonstrated performance, so waiting for it would make the prize depend on an administrative timetable. I would, however, concede that a prize cannot by wording alone remove the exclusion of ion-clock groups; the citation can only avoid claiming priority over them, and I think that is an honest limit and not a flaw in B012.

responses.point: Johansson accepts the two-name configuration but notes that priority for the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous proposals has not been verified, and asks whether the SI redefinition should come first.
responses.response: Priority is the one point on B012 that I cannot close from the supplied text, and I would not claim otherwise. My recollection is that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal was published as the founding concept and that other proposals for lattice-based clocks followed or ran in parallel, but that is a recollection and the committee should have the dated record in front of it before voting. I do not think the redefinition needs to come first, for the reason given to Kroll. On B038 I still treat the duplicate Ekert string as one person, and I accept your point that Ekert's entanglement route is a separate contribution, so Bennett and Brassard alone would be incomplete and the three names would unify two routes. That, with Wiesner, is why I do not see it competing with B012 this year.

responses.point: Olsson says the question of who is responsible for the original work has a short, defensible answer for B012, and that she would still support B022 if the Cao and Dean question is resolved.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and with your reading that a measurement taking performance to 10^-18 and changing what can be tested is a discovery of the same kind as a new phase. On B022 we agree that the open item is attribution, and I would add one practical consequence of your Cao and Dean question: if the committee checks the author record and finds that the first author of the 2018 papers carries a role equal to that of the group leader, a three-name cap makes B022 a different prize from the one on the supplied strings. I would keep the two configurations separate. I see no fair two-part prize combining B022 and B012 within three people, since any split would cut one side's credit unfairly, and I would not propose one.

uncertainties: Priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous lattice-clock proposals, and the relative weight of concept against demonstration, are from my recollection and not verified from the supplied text.

Whether the author and credit record of the first 2018 B022 papers (including Dean's group and the first author) can be examined well enough to settle whether the three supplied names are acceptable; my ranking of B022 second depends on it and could change.

Whether a citation worded around the lattice-clock architecture can avoid implying that trapped-ion clocks are of lesser standing, or whether some members would prefer an ion-clock name, which the three-person limit makes hard.

Whether eight years is enough for B022 given the open superconducting mechanism; I treat mechanism as separate from the discovery but cannot judge how colleagues in condensed matter weigh sample variability.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is documented. My connections are with Lindgren's Gothenburg group, Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and co-authors such as Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom is in my preferred configuration. I work in theoretical atomic physics, which is adjacent to optical-clock physics, so I disclose field proximity but no personal or institutional tie, as in round 1. No conflict arises for B022 or B018. If an attosecond or electron-ion collision part came up, I would disclose my collaborations.
